newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels ready to restart Lima hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels ready to restart Lima hostage talks.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages readied for the restart of direct talks as President Alberto Fujimori on Monday sought to assure British investors the two-month crisis had not hurt the country's viability.

Speaking in London, Fujimori also said on Monday there was no chance of a ransom being paid to 15 heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) hostage-takers holed up in the Japanese ambassador's house in Lima.
But he told BBC radio he was hopeful preliminary face-to-face talks slated to start on Tuesday could lead to a peaceful solution of the 55-day-old crisis.

"As a government we don't accept this kind of ransom payment. I think that all governments, not just Peruvian but around the world, must not accept these kinds of crimes and later pay ransom," he said.

Later in a speech at a forum on British investment in Latin America, Fujimori reiterated that the Dec. 17 seizure of the residence was an isolated event that did not affect the economy. He also insisted his government has crushed Peru's two leftist guerrilla groups.
The storming of the residence during a cocktail party attended by hundreds of VIPs "is not the product of organisations such as those that existed between 1980 and 1992," he said.

"Both the MRTA and Shining Path have been dismantled," Fujimori said. "Today there are still some terrorists, as there are in other countries, who seek to draw attention by committing atrocities without regard to human rights."
The speech was monitored in Lima on local radio, which carried it live in simultaneous translation.
Early on Sunday suspected Maoist Shining Path rebels tossed a package bomb at an electric company's offices in Lima, causing minor damage but no injuries, police said.

The Shining Path is larger than the Cuban-inspired MRTA and responsible for more of violence during Peru's 16 years of guerrilla wars. But it was overshadowed by the MRTA after the smaller group's spectacular seizure of the Japanese envoy's mansion 55 days ago.
In Lima the government and MRTA rebels led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini were to put the final touches on preparations for the resumption of preliminary face-to-face talks broken off Dec. 28.
On Sunday Fujimori announced government negotiator and Peru's education minister Domingo Palermo will meet with Cerpa's No. 2 Roli Rojas, known by his nom de guerre "El Arabe" - The Arab.
The private home across the street from the residence was prepared as the site of talks and an armoured van was readied to shuttle rebels to and from the negotiations.
But few expected talks to move quickly. "We hope the preliminary talks make enough progress to enter definitive talks, probably with Cerpa Crtolini himself," Fujimori said.

Direct talks snagged on Fujimori's refusal to discuss the rebels main demand -- the freeing of more than 400 comrades held in Peruvian jails. Despite repeated assurances he wanted to find a peaceful solution, the siege evolved into a tense standoff.
A breakthrough came last week when Roman Catholic Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani and two other mediators emerged from talks with Cerpa saying they were optimistic direct talks would be resumed.
Over the weekend, preparations moved ahead quietly for talks while concern in Lima over the weekend focused on the health of the hostages.
Despite medical visits arranged by the Red Cross, relatives of some hostages said their loved ones are ailing inside the residence.
